ATAM for agentic AI

An insurance claims case study: from a flexible agent to a defensible architecture.

The essential idea

Evaluate the whole system, not just the agent.

The Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (ATAM) evaluates architectural choices against competing quality goals. This worked example applies it to an AI assistant that answers insurance questions, collects claim details, processes documents and prepares actions for approval.

The result is a proposed shift from broad agent authority to a design with policy-gated tools, durable business state, grounded answers and enforceable human review. Each improvement carries a cost in latency, implementation effort or operational workload.

Case-study boundary: this is an illustrative system, not an assessment of a real insurance platform. Targets, ratings and pass conditions are proposed workshop inputs, not achieved results.

01 / Candidate design

Start with the business and the claim journey

SLIDE 01

ATAM in action

This worked example follows an insurance claims assistant from candidate design through architecture evaluation to risk-driven refinement. The system and its targets are illustrative, not the results of an actual insurer assessment.

SLIDE 02

Evaluate quality goals under stress

The architectural question is whether the system meets business-critical goals when conditions become difficult. Evaluate correctness, privacy, latency, reliability, traceability, cost and modifiability alongside its chat and document-processing capabilities.

SLIDE 03

One claim, seven responsibilities

A small auto-damage claim moves through understanding intent, answering policy questions, collecting details and consent, processing documents, checking rules and identity, escalating for approval, and closing the case. The assistant may prepare a recommendation; policy-defined controls govern financial and coverage decisions.

SLIDE 04

Business drivers before model selection

Workshop assumptions include a simple-FAQ p95 latency below three seconds, 99.9% availability for chat and claim status, zero unauthorized writes, and approval for every restricted action. These are proposed targets to validate with business owners, not measured outcomes.

SLIDE 05

Candidate A: a broad agent

The initial design gives one general-purpose agent responsibility for intent, reasoning, retrieval, document extraction, tool selection and responses. Claims APIs and human handoff sit downstream. The evaluation asks whether too much authority and responsibility are concentrated in the agent.

SLIDE 06

Six architectural choices

Compare agent topology, workflow ownership, autonomy, knowledge grounding, document processing and tool access. A general agent, specialist agents, a deterministic state machine, curated RAG, asynchronous jobs and a constrained gateway each create different quality tradeoffs.

02 / ATAM evaluation

Turn quality goals into testable scenarios

SLIDE 07

The nine ATAM steps

Present the method, business drivers and architecture; identify approaches, build the utility tree and analyze approaches; brainstorm and prioritize stakeholder scenarios, then re-analyze; finally present results. Experiments and prototypes supply evidence for the architectural analysis.

SLIDE 08

Who belongs in the workshop?

Include business owners, claims operations, architects, engineers, security, privacy, AI evaluation and legal or compliance stakeholders. Prepare the approval policy, ticket volumes, service targets and actual API permissions before the evaluation.

SLIDE 09

The quality-attribute utility tree

Translate broad goals into prioritized scenarios for performance, security, accuracy, reliability, oversight and cost. The deck labels scenarios by business importance and architectural difficulty: H/H means high importance and high difficulty, not a measured risk score.

SLIDE 10

A six-part quality scenario

Specify source, stimulus, environment, artifact, response and measure. In the example, a customer uploads a malicious PDF while a claim is open; ingestion, the agent and the gateway must treat its contents as data and deny unapproved writes. The test threshold is zero unauthorized state changes.

SLIDE 11

A prioritized scenario backlog

The backlog covers burst FAQ traffic, document prompt injection, cited coverage answers, interrupted OCR, high-value approval, cost spikes and a claims-rule change within 48 hours. Stakeholder voting determines which scenarios merit the first deep analysis.

SLIDE 12

S3: trustworthy coverage answers

Compare model-only answers, curated RAG and RAG with abstention. Approved versioned evidence improves grounding but adds retrieval overhead; abstaining on weak evidence adds staff workload. Collect grounded-answer, incorrect-answer and abstention rates alongside latency and freshness.

SLIDE 13

S2: authorization outside the model

An uploaded document can attempt to manipulate an overly privileged agent. In the guarded path, the LLM proposes an action and a policy gateway checks identity, action, scope and approval before a tool executes. Red-team testing must challenge this boundary.

SLIDE 14

S4: durable document processing

The proposed document path checks uploads, stores scoped encrypted evidence, queues durable jobs, extracts and validates fields, and updates cases with version and idempotency controls. Route low-confidence results to a human exception path and analyze failures after external side effects.

SLIDE 15

S1: an end-to-end latency budget

The illustrative three-second budget allocates 150 ms to input and authentication, 400 ms to retrieval, 1,550 ms to model response, 450 ms to tools and formatting, and 450 ms to network and margin. Extra agent hops and verification consume that budget; actual p95 behavior requires load testing.

SLIDE 16

S5: approval as durable workflow state

Draft, policy evaluation, pending approval, approved or denied, and execution are explicit states. Persist reviewer identity, rationale, approval version, timestamp, action payload and outcome so restarts or retries cannot bypass the approval requirement.

SLIDE 17

S4: recovery without duplicate actions

Persist the case ID before processing, retry OCR asynchronously with backoff, suppress repeated webhook writes through idempotency keys, and resume from durable state. Retry settings influence completion, duplicate-action risk, latency and cloud cost.

03 / Tradeoffs and risks

Make architectural consequences explicit

SLIDE 18

Compare alternatives without a universal winner

The deck contrasts a general agent, specialist agents and a guarded workflow. A general agent can simplify prototyping; specialization adds coordination and tracing work; guarded workflows emphasize isolation and auditable state. These qualitative ratings remain hypotheses until evaluated.

SLIDE 19

Autonomy tiers by business impact

The proposed T0–T3 pattern separates explanation, scoped reads, preparation of changes and restricted commits. Coverage, payment and other restricted actions require human and deterministic authorization. These tiers are a case-study proposal, not an industry-standard classification.

SLIDE 20

Sensitivity points and tradeoff points

A sensitivity point identifies a parameter with a strong effect on a quality, such as retrieval threshold or human queue capacity. A tradeoff point connects a decision to multiple qualities, such as an approval gate improving control while slowing completion. Confirm impacts with evidence.

SLIDE 21

An illustrative risk register

Six potential risks concern direct LLM write access, document instructions, missing durable state, weakly grounded answers, overloaded review queues and cost overruns. The proposed mitigations include a policy gateway, adversarial tests, idempotent workflows, abstention, capacity planning and budgets.

SLIDE 22

Risk themes and business impact

Group individual risks into uncontrolled agency, a fragile case lifecycle and unbounded operations. These themes link technical weaknesses to unsupported advice, duplicate service steps, longer resolution times and unsustainable staffing or model costs.

04 / Architecture refinement

Constrain execution and validate the result

SLIDE 23

Refined design: flexible conversation, deterministic control

The refined architecture separates identity and case APIs, durable workflow, AI orchestration and a policy tool gateway. Curated knowledge, sandboxed document processing and scoped claims APIs support the system. Audit, evaluation, tracing, cost limits and PII controls cut across the design.

SLIDE 24

Record the accepted tradeoffs

Replace direct API calls with a gateway, inline document work with queued extraction, model-generated state with a workflow store, and free-form answers with versioned RAG and abstention. Persist approvals and bound steps, costs and timeouts. Each change brings overhead that should be explicitly accepted.

SLIDE 25

Close risks with measurable evidence

Load-test latency, red-team authorization, review grounded answers, interrupt workers, repeat webhooks, attempt approval bypasses and measure cost per completed request. Do not close a risk until the agreed acceptance evidence exists.

SLIDE 26

An evidence-led workshop playbook

Prepare business drivers, diagrams, quality metrics, policies and sample journeys one to two weeks ahead. Use the first workshop day for initial analysis and the second for stakeholder scenarios and deeper challenges. Follow up with risk themes, decision records and verification tests.

SLIDE 27

From agent demo to architecture discipline

Choose an architecture whose tradeoffs are explicit, testable and acceptable to stakeholders. The case study recommends autonomous conversation, constrained execution, durable workflow and accountable decisions.

Questions, answered

ATAM and agentic AI FAQ

What is ATAM?

The Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method is a structured approach to evaluating architecture against competing quality goals. It identifies risks, sensitivity points and tradeoff points through business drivers and concrete scenarios.

How does ATAM apply to agentic AI?

Evaluate model and tool behavior within the complete system: authorization, retrieval, workflow state, human approval, failure recovery, latency and cost. Use scenarios to test whether architectural choices meet stakeholder goals.

What changed in the refined architecture?

Replace direct API calls with a gateway, inline document work with queued extraction, model-generated state with a workflow store, and free-form answers with versioned RAG and abstention. Persist approvals and bound steps, costs and timeouts. Each change brings overhead that should be explicitly accepted.

Does the case study prove the performance targets?

No. The service targets, latency budget, risk ratings and architecture comparisons are illustrative assumptions. The proposed design needs workload-specific experiments and operational evidence.

Are more agents always better?

No. Specialist agents can improve separation of responsibilities, but introduce coordination, latency and distributed tracing overhead. Select a topology using prioritized scenarios and evidence.

Why must approval persist outside the model?

Approval must remain enforceable through retries, restarts and repeated events. A deterministic workflow and gateway can bind an authorized reviewer’s decision to a specific action and version.
